paper_sections.title: Ghrelin Modulates Brain Activity in Areas that Control Appetitive Behavior

description.value: The study examined whether intravenous ghrelin enhances the neural response to food pictures relative to scenery pictures in healthy nonobese men, and whether ghrelin-related brain responses are associated with hunger and subsequent recognition of food images.

design.value: Twenty healthy medication-free normal weight male subjects underwent a single fMRI session three hours after a standardized breakfast. Twelve subjects viewed food and scenery pictures before and after single-blinded intravenous ghrelin administration, while eight subjects underwent the same two-block paradigm without ghrelin as a control/control experiment.

description.value: Subjects answered questions regarding their appetite, including “how hungry are you right now?”, on a 10 point visual analog scale at the start and end of each block.
Visual analog scales rating mood, including irritable, nauseous, and bored, were completed before and after breakfast and at the beginning and end of the imaging blocks.
Approximately 30 min after scanning, subjects saw the 45 food images viewed in the scanner intermixed with 26 novel food images and stated whether each image had been seen while in the scanner.
Subjects rated the images approximately 30 min after scanning on a scale of 1 to 9, where 1 = “extremely dislike” and 9 = “extremely like.”

task_description.value: During each 5 min functional run, 15 images, consisting of 7–8 food and 7–8 scenery pictures, were presented in random order. Each picture was shown for 5 s followed by a 15 s dark screen with a central fixation cross. Subjects were instructed to focus their attention on the stimuli. The functional protocol consisted of two blocks, each containing three functional runs.

description.value: T2* weighted images with BOLD contrast were acquired. Thirty-two 4 mm thick slices covered the whole brain. The functional session consisted of six runs of 5 min, each consisting of 100 volumes per run. Two dummy images were taken at the onset of each sequence and discarded to reduce non-steady state effects.

Functional images were spatially smoothed with a 6 mm Gaussian filter and motion corrected prior to statistical analyses. Parametric images were transformed into Montreal Neurological Institute space.

model_settings.value: Separate regressors for food and scenery pictures consisting of boxcar functions convolved with a standard hemodynamic response function; the food minus scenery contrast was computed for each individual.

estimator.value: A t statistic was calculated from the effect size and standard deviation of the general linear model for each individual.

model_settings.value: Group analysis was performed on individual parametric images transformed into Montreal Neurological Institute space. Multiple comparisons were corrected using the entire brain search volume, the amount of smoothing, and the degrees of freedom; regions were listed when they contained clusters with p < 0.001 and volume greater than 100 ml.
The interaction effect was generated as ([ghrelin − control] − [control 2 − control 1]).
A paired t test was used to compare behavioral and hormonal measures in the ghrelin and control conditions.
